newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Police contain small Albania investor rallies.
newsitem.headline: Police contain small Albania investor rallies.

text.p: Police were out in force on Sunday to watch over rallies by the handful of Albanians bold enough to press demands for the dismissal of the right-wing government and compensation for savings lost in failed pyramid schemes.

But residents of Europe's poorest country were clearly cowed by a crackdown last week after violent protests in which enraged investors set fire to government buildings. Many ruined would-be demonstrators chose this time to stay home.
In Tirana, scores of uniformed and plainclothes police cordoned off roads leading to a soccer pitch where a trade union rally was to have taken place.

Its main organiser, Azem Hajdari, one of the heroes of the campaign that toppled hardline communists in 1990, was manhandled and briefly detained by police. Police said organisers had failed to obtain the necessary permission.
About 500 people turned out for a demonstration in a stadium in the Adriatic port of Durres. Police swarmed around the area on foot and in vans but kept their distance.
Albanian state television showed an even smaller number gathered in a stadium in Lezhe, further to the north.

Television also broadcast for the second day running a stream of interviews with ordinary Albanians denouncing last week's violence. An Italian investor followed, telling an interviewer he was undeterred by the disturbances.

In Tirana, Hajdari told a news conference the government had banned his rally because it was trying to persuade Albanians that only communists lay behind the protests against the collapse of the investment schemes.
"I am telling them they have lost the people's confidence. The Albanian people are better than their government which should resign without delay," he said.
"It is time for them to weigh their moves carefully or they will find themselves checkmated."
Hajdari accuses the government of failing to warn Albanians of the dangers of the schemes despite one collapse as early as 1992. But he remains close to President Sali Berisha.
Virtually every Albanian family had a stake in the schemes, which impressed uninitiated investors with regular interest payments until they began to collapse in recent months.
The president has promised that the poorest investors in two of the dubious plans will start getting compensation this week, some in cash, others in government certificates.
Hajdari was among student leaders who led protests against the communists who inherited power from hardliner Enver Hoxha, who kept the Balkan nation in isolation for 40 years.
Albanians are clearly wary after the arrest of nearly 150 people on public order charges following last weekend's protests. Prosecutors say those convicted could face at least 15 years in prison.
Thousands demonstrated in central Tirana last Sunday, hurling stones and clashing with riot police.
One elderly man in Durres said there were three reasons why so few people had attended the latest rally.

"Firstly, there were so many police outside the stadium, secondly because the Democrats here have warned people that if they demonstrate they will lose their state jobs, and thirdly, because of the arrests," he said.
